pamphlet_excerpts: Lightning Protocol: Move the craft immediately to shore whenever thunder rumbles across the water.
Cold Water Shock: Sudden immersion initiates an involuntary gasp reflex that leads to immediate drowning.
Strainers And Obstacles: River currents force small rowboats against submerged trees causing rapid swamping.
Blister Mitigation: Friction tape applied to tender palm pressure points prevents severe skin tears.
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Weather Assessment: Check local marine forecasts and atmospheric pressure trends before launching the craft.

Step 3 - First Aid Check: Pack waterproof medical supplies for treating abrasions, blisters, hypothermia, and heat exhaustion.
Step 4 - Float Plan Filing: Deliver a detailed route schedule and passenger manifest to onshore leadership personnel.

pamphlet_excerpts: Continuous Swim Distance: Complete one hundred yards continuously with seventy-five yards using strong forward strokes.
Resting Backstroke Stage: Finish the final twenty-five yards using an easy, restful elementary backstroke.
Deep Water Entry: Jump feet first into deep water and submerge before starting the swim.
Floating Endurance Demonstration: Maintain a stationary floating or resting position for sixty seconds without forward movement.
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Feet First Jump: Plunge feet first into water over head height and surface smoothly.
Step 2 - Forward Propulsion: Swim seventy-five yards continuously using an effective side, breast, or crawl stroke.
Step 3 - Backstroke Recovery: Complete the final twenty-five yards using a relaxed and restful elementary backstroke.
Step 4 - Stationary Float: Rest motionlessly on your back for one full minute without paddling feet.

pamphlet_excerpts: Type Three Approval: Choose inherently buoyant vest designs that permit unrestricted arm and shoulder motion.
Strap Tensioning Sequence: Tighten lower torso straps first before snugging shoulder adjusters to anchor foam.
Shoulder Lift Test: Pull upward on vest shoulder panels to confirm the neckline stays below ears.
Permanent Wear Rule: Fasten the life jacket securely before stepping off docks into any rowboat.
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Label Examination: Check the manufacturer label for United States Coast Guard approval and user weight.
Step 2 - Vest Loosening: Loosen all adjustment webbing before placing your arms through the armholes properly.
Step 3 - Buckle Fastening: Close the front zipper and buckle all torso straps starting from waist level.
Step 4 - Snugness Check: Have a buddy pull upward on shoulder straps to test proper torso retention.

Step 4 - Backwater Course: Push both oars together to back the rowboat fifty yards along a line.

pamphlet_excerpts: Blade Feathering Benefit: Turning oar blades flat parallel to water reduces headwind resistance on recovery.
Rough Water Handling: Quarter your boat diagonally into breaking waves to prevent capsizing or swamping.
Oar Sizing Formula: Calculate proper oar length using half the boat beam width plus leverage.
Full Body Conditioning: Rowing engages quadriceps, gluteals, latissimus dorsi, and core muscles in rhythmic cycles.
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Feathering Drill: Rotate wrists downward at stroke completion to turn the blade horizontal smoothly.
Step 2 - Rough Water Heading: Steer the hull into wave troughs at a steady forty-five degree angle.
Step 3 - Winterizing Hull: Clean bilge debris, wash salt deposits, and store the boat inverted undercover.
Step 4 - Ergometer Session: Row twenty minutes maintaining target heart rates to develop aerobic stamina and endurance.

left_points: (9a) Oar Blade Feathering Mechanics: Feathering rotates the oar blade horizontal to the water surface during the recovery stroke. This aerodynamic maneuver minimizes wind resistance and reduces the hazard of blades catching wave crests.

(9b) Heavy Weather Boat Handling Precautions: High winds and crashing waves can rapidly overwhelm small rowboats through windward drifting or swamping. Rowers preserve stability by quartering into seas, ballasting weight low, and heading toward leeward shores.

(9c) Seasonal Boat Maintenance And Storage: Spring fitting out requires checking hardware tightness, repairing hull gelcoat, and oiling moving oarlock sockets. Winter storage demands thorough cleaning, drying, and sheltering the hull inverted off bare soil.
right_points: (9d) Proper Oar Length Determination: Oar length must match the rowboat beam width between oarlocks to ensure proper mechanical leverage. Handbooks recommend dividing the beam by two, adding two inches, and multiplying by seven-fifths.

(9e) Fixed Versus Sliding Seat Rowing: Fixed-seat craft utilize stationary thwarts that rely on back and arm power for hull propulsion. Sliding-seat shells feature rolling seats and foot stretchers that recruit major leg muscle groups.

(9f) Dual Meanings Of Sculling Terminology: In traditional boating, sculling refers to propelling a craft with a single stern oar. In competitive rowing, sculling describes rowing with two individual oars per person simultaneously.

rows.right: (9d) Calculating Proper Oar Length: Remember to keep sight of the person who needs help and to push the bow of the boat in the direction you want (p. 67).

B. Downwind with the waves pushing the stern at maximum speed.
C. Broadside to the wind and waves so the boat drifts sideways into the swimmer.
D. With both oars shipped inside the boat while coasting with the current.
choices: A. Into the wind or against the current to maintain precise control of the boat.
B. Downwind with the waves pushing the stern at maximum speed.
C. Broadside to the wind and waves so the boat drifts sideways into the swimmer.

quiz_item.correct_answer: A. Into the wind or against the current to maintain precise control of the boat.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (A): Approaching a swimmer into the wind or against the current gives the rower much better control over speed and alignment when stopping at the person in the water (p. 67).

patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (D): Rowers face backward and must glance over their shoulder every few strokes to watch for hazards, always wear a USCG-approved PFD under Safety Afloat, and stay with a swamped boat rather than swimming far to shore.

patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): In a rowboat swimmer rescue, you row out to the swimmer, pivot the boat, and back the stern within reach while giving clear instructions so they can hold the transom for a tow to shore (p. 79).
